review_method: Read all132 complete actual source units in two full chapter groups13–14 and15–16. Read all proposed retained target passages and necessary context, then separately reread all135 complete source/target/category/rationale triples in four untruncated groups1–35,36–70,71–105 and106–135. Preserved the initial draft and eight exact explanation/category refinements (seven author precisions and one independent peer suggestion about approaching to bow); separately reread all eight corrected complete triples. External contexts included Genesis4:1–15 and34:1–7, Leviticus18:6–11, Numbers27:1–7, Job2:1–10 including2:9a–e, Matthew1:6–8, 2Chronicles11:18–22, 1Kings1:1–6 and2:8–9, Ruth1:14–18, John18:1–3, 1Samuel14:42–45 and26:6–9, Psalms108:26–31, and necessary 2Samuel3/8/9/12/17/19 context. Connections use particular stated commands and responses, repeated descriptions, family relationships, contrasting speeches and narrative reports. Original wording, numbers, conditional claims, ambiguous pronouns and different names are preserved. This is an initial curated supplied-English pass, not exhaustive discovery or new Greek/Hebrew/apparatus work, specialist verification, modern geography or solved historical harmonization.

old_row.relationship: The narrated sibling violation beside the explicit kinship prohibition
old_row.rationale: The narrative describes Amnon violating the woman he and she have called his sister; Leviticus forbids uncovering a sister's nakedness, from either parent. Tamar's earlier proposal to consult the king is not recast as an exception to that law.

new_row.relationship: The narrated sibling violation beside the explicit kinship prohibition
new_row.rationale: The narrative describes Amnon violating Tamar, whom he calls his sister and who calls him her brother; Leviticus forbids uncovering a sister's nakedness, from either parent. Tamar's earlier proposal to consult the king is not recast as an exception to that law.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter Absalom's two distinct silences follow the violation
old_row.rationale: Absalom tells Tamar to be silent and not set her heart on speaking, while the later notice says he speaks neither evil nor good to Amnon because he hates him for violating her. The narrated as-widow residence is not rewritten into a separately established marriage history.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed Tamar-Maacah maternal-name identity; no identity credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: The full source names Tamar, Absalom's daughter, as Rehoboam's wife and Abijah's mother. Chronicles names Maacah daughter of Absalom as mother of Abijah in Rehoboam's family context. Both passages and necessary context were read; the differently named mothers are not independently equated. The same retained passage pair credits only the explicit common Rehoboam-Abijah paternal relationship, not the disputed maternal identity.
unresolved_candidates.retained_pair_scope: Rehoboam-Abijah paternity only; maternal-name equivalence excluded

candidate_exclusions.proposed_claim: Equate Tamar with Maacah; substitute familiar illness, kinship, timeline, clothing, numbers, names, geography or pronouns; turn presented cases, political accusations, conditional hopes or counsel into independently established facts.
candidate_exclusions.reason: Retained comparisons follow the complete supplied clauses and explicit distinctions. The maternal-name identity remains pending with zero identity credit; no standalone unsupported pair or harmonization is added.

editorial_notes.note: Preserve the narrator's illness wording alongside Jonadab's act-ill advice; wrist-reaching sleeves; Tamar as-widow wording; the king's spirit ceased going after Absalom; the coached case and positive God-takes-life/banishment clauses; the two full years in14:28 and unspecified hair-cut interval in14:26 without invented dating; expanded14:27; forty years15:7; Baithar, Roos, Gola and Araboth; separate fathers of the two named sons; dates rather than imported figs; speakers' accusations and divine-command attributions; wives versus concubines and counsel reputation without universal moral approval.
